rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir reads الرياح in the plural here and at four other places, using singular الريح elsewhere in the listed set.
rows.anchor: في البقرة هاهنا [الآية/ 164] وفي الحجر

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nafi reads الرياح in the plural in twelve locations, including this verse; Abu Amr, Asim, and Ibn Amir also have the plural here.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع: الرياح في اثني عشر موضعا

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisai read the singular here: Hamza pluralizes only two other locations, while al-Kisai adds al-Hijr 15:22 to those two.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة الرياح على الجمع في موضعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qays describe four principal winds—north, south, east, and west—and call a wind between two directions a nakba; Abu Zayd illustrates the east wind with poetry.
rows.anchor: قال القيسيون الرياح أربع: الشمال والجنوب والصبا والدبور

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-A'rabi locates the south, east, north, and west winds by the rising or setting points of Suhayl, the Pleiades, and Banat Na'sh.
rows.anchor: فأما مهبهن فإن ابن الأعرابي قال: مهب الجنوب

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Asma'i gives a different compass description: south runs from Suhayl to dawn, north faces it, and the winds from behind and opposite the Kaaba are west and east.
rows.anchor: وقال الأصمعي ما بين سهيل إلى طرف بياض الفجر جنوب

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي والأصمعي
rows.claim: A wind between two named winds is a nakba; al-Asma'i also applies the term when one of the four veers from its course, with plural nakb.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأعرابي: كل ريح بين ريحين فهي نكباء

rows.speaker: الطوسي
rows.claim: Another account places the south from Yemen and north from Syria, calls south al-Azyab or al-Na‘ama, and gives north the names Mahwa and Jarbiya.
rows.anchor: قال الطوسي: وقال غير الأصمعي وابن الأعرابي: الجنوب التي تجيء من قبل اليمن

rows.speaker: الطوسي
rows.claim: The hot, drying quality called hayf belongs to the south and west winds; north and east do not have it.
rows.anchor: والجنوب والدبور لهما هيف

rows.speaker: الطوسي
rows.claim: Mahwa is a name for the north wind because it wipes away and disperses clouds; other names include مسعا and نسعا.
rows.anchor: سميت محوة لأنها تمحو السحاب وتذهب به

rows.speaker: الطوسي
rows.claim: The sterile wind does not pollinate clouds; pollinating winds stir clouds by God's permission and fertilize trees, while ذاريات winds scatter dust.
rows.anchor: العقيم: التي لا تلقح السحاب

rows.speaker: الطرماح
rows.claim: In al-Tirmah's وصف, a pollinating wind is the south and a barren one is the north; the adjectives mean possessing fertilization or its opposite, not active participles.
rows.anchor: يريد بالحيال أنها لا تلقح كما تلقح الجنوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In الحجر 15:22 لواقح means ملاقح (fertilizing winds or winds that are fertilized); the form omits an augment, as poetry also omits it in a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وأرسلنا الرياح لواقح [الحجر/ 22] والمعنى فيه: ملاقح

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: People dislike the cold north wind because it removes clouds, but welcome the warm south wind for bringing clouds, rain, fertility, and relief.
rows.anchor: يكرهون الشمال لبردها وذهابها بالغيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase للقح الجنوب is parsed as لإلقاح الجنوب, with the augment omitted from the verbal noun and the noun annexed to its agent.
rows.anchor: قوله: «للقح الجنوب» تقديره: لإلقاح الجنوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural وتصريف الرياح is clearest because each wind equally signifies divine oneness and is directed for people's benefit; a singular may still denote the generic wind.
rows.anchor: كل واحدة من هذه الرياح مثل الأخرى في دلالتها على الوحدانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If all winds were subjected to Solomon, الريح signals their multitude; if one particular wind was subjected, the singular is definite by reference.
rows.anchor: فإن كانت الرياح كلها سخرت له، فالمراد بها الكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wind sent against ‘Ad and the wind sent against the Confederates was one wind, supported by verses and the report that the east wind aided the Prophet while the west wind destroyed ‘Ad.
rows.anchor: وفي عاد إذ أرسلنا عليهم الريح العقيم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet prayed for a wind to come as plural winds rather than a singular wind; al-Farisi takes this to distinguish mercy from punishment.
rows.anchor: اللهم اجعلها رياحا ولا تجعلها ريحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Plural winds suit mercy and singular wind punishment: he links the prayer to the merciful herald winds in al-Rum and the singular sterile wind sent to ‘Ad.
rows.anchor: مواضع الرحمة بالجمع أولى، ومواضع العذاب بالإفراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wind can denote a generic class containing both mercy and punishment; as a generic noun it can refer to all winds or only some members, as in the passage about passing by the people of Lot.
rows.anchor: فإذا كانت للجنس كان على القبيلين العذاب والرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Quranic usage, وما يدريك normally leaves the matter unspecified, whereas وما أدراك is followed by an explanation; he cites the Hour and the Resurrection as examples.
rows.anchor: وما يدريك مبهم غير مبين

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وعاصم
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Nafi, and Asim pronounce the ث clearly in كم لبثت and لبثتم throughout the Quran.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير ونافع وعاصم في كل القرآن ذلك بإظهار الثاء

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisai assimilate ث into ت throughout the Quran.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي بالإدغام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Clear pronunciation follows from the sounds' differing articulation zones; assimilation treats them as near-identical because they share tongue-tip contact and voicelessness, and ت is a subject suffix bound like part of the word.
rows.anchor: من بين لبثت ولم يدغم، فلتباين المخرجين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assimilation is supported by ست, where Arabic assimilates dāl to ت despite their voicing difference, and by the assimilation of the middle of وتد in a variant.
rows.anchor: فبحسب إلزامهم الإدغام في هذه الكلمة مع اختلاف الحرفين في الجهر والهمس

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر
rows.claim: These readers retain ه in liaison in all five listed words, including لم يتسنه; everyone retains it at pause.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر هذه الحروف كلها

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza deletes the h in liaison from all five words; al-Kisai deletes it in لم يتسنه and اقتده but retains it in the other three.
rows.anchor: وكان حمزة يحذفهن في الوصل. وكان الكسائي يحذف الهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: سنة has two senses: a year or a drought, the opposite of fertility; the following discussion uses the drought sense to explain the verse's word.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: السنة تستعمل على ضربين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase عام السنة must mean a drought year, since reading it as a year of years would be tautological; poetry uses سنون for barren years.
rows.anchor: فلا يكون الأول لأنه يلزم أن يكون التقدير

rows.speaker: أوس
rows.claim: Aws describes the years around his land after the sacred month as drought-stricken and barren, glossing تلمع as lacking fertility and vegetation.
rows.anchor: وما حولها جدب سنون تلمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word سنين has several plural patterns; the form in poetry is not a vocative truncation, but a plural like مأنة ومئون, with easing for rhyme.
rows.anchor: وإنما أراد بالسني: جمع فعلة على فعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: لم يتسنه may derive from a noun ending in h, from سنة as in أسنتوا/سنوات, or from مسنون meaning changed, with an n assimilated or inverted.
rows.anchor: لم يتسنه [البقرة/ 259] فيحتمل ضربين

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو الشيباني
rows.claim: Abu Amr al-Shaybani is reported to favor deriving لم يتسنه from سنة; on the proposed pause-h analyses its h should appear at pause and drop in connected speech.
rows.anchor: ويحكى أن أبا عمرو الشيباني إلى هذا كان يذهب في هذا الحرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Retaining h in liaison is grammatically sound if h is the final radical of سنة, just as a final h remains in لم ينقه زيد and لم يجبه عمرو.
rows.anchor: فإن ذلك مستقيم في قياس العربية في يتسنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In اقتده, h can be a pronoun for the verbal noun: the command means اقتد الاقتداء, with the verbal noun supplied by the verb's meaning.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن تكون الهاء كناية عن المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For ماليه, سلطانيه, and هيه, deleting h in liaison better fits Arabic; retaining it is also defensible when a complete phrase is treated like a rhyme at pause.
rows.anchor: فالإسقاط للهاء في الدرج أوجه في قياس العربية

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Hamza's deletion of all pause-h letters in liaison is strongest: if some people treat rhymes as ordinary speech, unmetered speech has even less reason to imitate rhymes.
rows.anchor: وقول حمزة في ذلك أسد

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisai takes a middle course, deleting h from يتسنه and اقتده but retaining it in the three phrase-final words; both choices are permissible.
rows.anchor: والكسائي قد وافق حمزة في حذف الهاء

rows.speaker: أحمد بن موسى
rows.claim: Readers agree on h in كتابيه and حسابيه in liaison; this supports making phrase endings rhyme-like, not following the spelling of the codex.
rows.anchor: ولم يختلفوا في كتابيه وحسابيه أنها بالهاء في الوصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Writing final tāʾ as h cannot explain pause-h readings: if script controlled pronunciation, feminine tāʾ and written alif elsewhere would also persist in liaison.
rows.anchor: فلو كان ذلك للخط، لوجب أن تجعل تاءات التأنيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh records ثلاثة أربعة with a pause-like h in liaison; Abu Amr's clear n in ياسين والقرآن likewise reflects intending a pause between letter names.
rows.anchor: حكى في العدد أنهم يقولون: ثلاثة أربعة

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh does not treat such rare forms as productive analogies; extending them beyond number words and letter names would overgeneralize exceptional patterns.
rows.anchor: وسيبويه لا يعتد بهذه الشواذ ولا يقيس عليها

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: They read ننشرها with first nūn damma and rāʾ; نشر in this reading means revive the bones, as in Quranic descriptions of resurrection.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو: ننشرها

rows.speaker: عاصم وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: These four read ننشزها with zāy; another report from Asim gives a rāʾ reading with an open first nūn and damma on shīn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي: ننشزها بالزاي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rāʾ reading means revive: نشر, resurrection, and sending forth are close in sense, and wind too is described as spreading or bringing life.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: من قال: كيف ننشرها

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abu Zayd glosses أنشر الله الريح as sending it forth; the author relates this 'raising' to Quranic uses of baath and irsal for reviving.
rows.anchor: قال أبو زيد: أنشر الله الريح إنشارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reported Asim reading ننشرها with open first nūn and damma on shīn can be causative, like drying the animal or lowering water, or can depict unfolding what death had folded.
rows.anchor: فأما ما روي عن عاصم من قوله: كيف ننشرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The zāy reading ننشزها means raise the bones, bringing them together for revival; نشوز is a wife's turning away from marital accord, a related sense of rising apart.
rows.anchor: فتقدير ننشزها نرفع بعضها إلى بعض للإحياء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر
rows.claim: They read قال أعلم with a separate, hamzated alif and damma on mīm, as a statement: after witnessing revival, the speaker declares certain knowledge of God's power.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر: قال أعلم

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They join the hamza and read أعلم as an imperative, 'Know that God is capable of everything'; its force still amounts to a declaration of certainty.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي: قال أعلم أن الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imperative addresses the speaker's own soul as if it were another person, a recognized Arabic rhetorical practice illustrated with poetic self-address.
rows.anchor: ينزل أحدهم نفسه منزلة الأجنبي

rows.speaker: عاصم وابن عامر
rows.claim: Asim and Ibn Amir read بربوة with fatḥa on rāʾ in this verse and in al-Mu'minun; Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Abu Amr, Hamza, and al-Kisai use ḍamma.
rows.anchor: فقرأ عاصم وابن عامر: بربوة بفتح الراء

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan prefers ربوة with ḍamma and no alif; al-Farisi supports him because its plural is ربى and it derives from rising above the surrounding ground.
rows.anchor: والذي نختار: ربوة، بضم الراء وحذف الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Riba has a prohibited form—excess in exchanging like weighed or measured goods—and a disliked, non-prohibited form of giving a gift while expecting more back.
rows.anchor: ومنه الربا، وهو على ضربين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 30:39, gift-riba earns no divine reward like sincere charity; وما آتيتم من ربا may be either a conditional clause or a relative clause, with different grammatical constructions.
rows.anchor: وما آتيتم من ربا ليربوا في أموال الناس فلا يربوا عند الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If وما آتيتم من زكاة is a relative clause, its predicate is فأولئك هم المضعفون; the omitted resumptive pronoun is understood, and the discourse shifts from address to third person.
rows.anchor: وقال: وما آتيتم من زكاة ثم قال: فأولئك هم المضعفون

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima explains ولا تمنن تستكثر as forbidding a gift given in order to receive more in return.
rows.anchor: سمعت عكرمة يقول: «ولا تمنن تستكثر» قال: لا تعط شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative تستكثر can describe a future condition or an intended state, but a jussive reading has no semantic fit: the verse does not prohibit giving for the sake of getting more.
rows.anchor: فأما رفع تستكثر فعلى ضربين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For فصرهن in the adjacent bird passage, one interpretation is 'cut them up,' requiring no omitted verb; another is 'incline them,' with إليك attaching to خذ or to the turning verb.
rows.anchor: ومن قدر: فصرهن أو فصرهن، أنه بمعنى: قطعهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If فصرهن means incline them, Sibawayh's syntax attaches إليك to the nearer verb; attaching it to خذ is also possible, with an object understood for the later verb.
rows.anchor: وقياس قول سيبويه: أن يكون متعلقا بقطعهن

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: They lighten the kāf in أكلها when annexed to a feminine noun; Abu Amr alone uses the heavier form for masculine annexes and unannexed forms, while Nafi and Ibn Kathir lighten those too.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو ونافع أكلها [البقرة/ 265] خفيفة

rows.speaker: عاصم وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: These readers use a heavy kāf in أكلها, أكل, and أكله; lexical evidence shows أكل can mean edible produce, in contrast to the verbal noun of eating.
rows.anchor: وقرأها عاصم وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي: أكلها، والأكل، وأكله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that the garden yields twice its usual produce confirms that أكل here means what is eaten, namely its produce.
rows.anchor: وقوله: فآتت أكلها ضعفين [البقرة/ 265] فيه دلالة

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan distinguishes أكل as the food eaten from أكل as the act of eating; أَكلة can mean one meal, while اُكلة can mean food.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الحسن: الأكل ما يؤكل، والأكل: الفعل

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abu Zayd says a person described as ذو أكل has a share of worldly livelihood and provision.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو زيد: يقال إنه لذو أكل

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: They read ولا يحسبن الذين يبخلون with yāʾ and kasra on sīn; across the cited verses their third-person readings keep the named group as the subject.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو: ولا يحسبن الذين كفروا

rows.speaker: نافع وابن عامر
rows.claim: Nafi and Ibn Amir use yāʾ for the first clauses, but tāʾ for فلا تحسبنهم; Nafi has kasra and Ibn Amir fatḥa on sīn in that final form.
rows.anchor: غير أن نافعا كسر السين وفتحها ابن عامر

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Hamza reads the cited clauses about disbelievers and those who rejoice with tāʾ, opening both bāʾ and sīn; the form addresses the Prophet directly.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة: ولا تحسبن الذين كفروا

rows.speaker: عاصم والكسائي
rows.claim: Asim and al-Kisai read most forms in the sura with tāʾ, but use yāʾ in the clauses about hoarders and disbelievers; they differ in the vowel of sīn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم والكسائي كل ما في هذه السورة بالتاء إلا حرفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With yāʾ, الذين is the subject and the clause that follows can fill both objects of حسب; ما can mean 'that which' or function as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: الذين في هذه الآي في قراءتهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ولا يحسبن الذين يبخلون, the hoarders are the subject, the first object (البخل) is omitted but understood, and هو separates it from خيرًا لهم.
rows.anchor: فالذين يبخلون فاعل يحسبن والمفعول الأول محذوف من اللفظ

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan dislikes the yāʾ reading for the next clauses because حسب is left without an expressed object, although it often takes two.
rows.anchor: لا يعجبني قراءة من قرأ الأولى بالياء، لأنه لم يوقعه

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: They read والله بما يعملون خبير with yāʾ, continuing the third-person reference to those who hoard; God knows their withholding of due rights and requites it.
rows.anchor: أن من قرأ بالياء أتبعه ما قبله، وهو على الغيبة

rows.speaker: باقون
rows.claim: The other readers use tāʾ, linking the clause to the preceding address وإن تؤمنوا وتتقوا and referring to the believers' righteous work.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ بالتاء فلأن قبله خطابا، وهو قوله: وإن تؤمنوا وتتقوا

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn Amir alone repeats bāʾ in بالبينات وبالزبر, as in Syrian codices; the other readers omit the second bāʾ because conjunction already carries the preposition.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر وحده: بالبينات وبالزبر [آل عمران/ 184] بالباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating bāʾ is valid for emphasis, as repeated nouns appear in poetry; both the repeated-preposition and shared-preposition constructions are sound Arabic.
rows.anchor: ووجه قول ابن عامر أن إعادة الباء، وإن كان مستغنى عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage gives competing forms of ليميز: a light reading is connected with ماز يميز and the heavy form with ميزته فتميز; its reciter list appears internally inconsistent, naming Hamza and al-Kisai and then all others for the same heavy form.
rows.anchor: ليميز الله [الأنفال/ 37] بفتح الياء خفيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavy form is supported by Quranic تميز: objects separate through repeated movement and agitation; the phrase من الغيظ depicts the intensity of the boiling, angry fire.
rows.anchor: لأن التميز انفصال بعض الأشياء من بعض

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nafi's transmitters vary in how they render آلآن: some ask it with one hamza, while Warsh lengthens the initial hamza, opens lām, and omits the second hamza by transferring its vowel.
rows.anchor: مد الهمزة الأولى، ولا يهمز بعد اللام

rows.speaker: باقون
rows.claim: The other readers retain the hamza after lām and keep lām quiescent; reports from Qalun also describe a single hamza followed by lengthening.
rows.anchor: والباقون يهمزون بعد اللام واللام ساكنة [الآن]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the definite article precedes an initial hamza that is lightened, Arabic may transfer its vowel to lām and keep hamzat al-waṣl, or delete hamzat al-waṣl; both pronunciations have evidence.
rows.anchor: إن لام المعرفة إذا دخلت على كلمة أولها

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read دأبًا with a quiescent hamza; Abu Amr drops the hamza when reciting in connected flow.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر، وحمزة، والكسائي: دأبا ساكنة الهمزة

rows.speaker: حفص عن عاصم
rows.claim: Hafs reports دأبًا with fatḥa on hamza, whereas Abu Bakr reports it quiescent; the source also records a fatḥa transmission from Asim.
rows.anchor: وروى حفص عن عاصم: دأبا بفتح الهمزة. وروى أبو بكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quiescence is the more common form; fatḥa may be a dialect variant like شمع/شمع, and دأبًا is accusative after تزرعون.
rows.anchor: الأكثر في دأب* الإسكان، ولعل الفتح لغة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر
rows.claim: They read يعصرون in the third person, with the people previously mentioned as its subject.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر: يعصرون بالياء

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read تعصرون in the second person, addressing the petitioners who asked Joseph for an interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي: تعصرون بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb can mean pressing oil or juice in the coming fertile year; some interpreters say the people had gone fourteen years without pressing oil or grapes, while another sense is escaping to safety.
rows.anchor: وهذا يمكن أن يكون تأويل الآية عليه ، لأن من المتأولين

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda glosses تعصرون as نجاة (being saved); poetry and related usages support العصر as a refuge or means of escape.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: تعصرون: تنجون

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir reads إنك لأنت يوسف as a statement; all others make it a question, supported by Joseph's answer and the reported wording أو أنت يوسف؟ in Ubayy's codex.
rows.anchor: وكلهم قرأ: أإنك لأنت يوسف [90] بالاستفهام غير ابن كثير

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وعاصم وابن عامر
rows.claim: They pronounce two hamzas in أإنك; the remaining readers use one, according to their usual rules for two adjacent hamzas.
rows.anchor: فكان حمزة والكسائي وعاصم وابن عامر: يهمزون همزتين

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir alone, through Qunbul, retains yāʾ in يتقي in both liaison and pause; the other readers omit it in both contexts.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وحده: إنه من يتقي ويصبر [90] بياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The retained yāʾ in ويتقي ويصبر can coordinate on the semantic position of the conditional response; alternatively, its vowel may be omitted for ease, as in other Quranic and poetic forms.
rows.anchor: والآخر: أن يجعل من يتقي بمنزلة: الذي يتقي

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan reports hearing رسلنا لديهم with a quiescent lām; this supports easing the vowel before فإن الله in the reading ويصبر.
rows.anchor: وزعم أبو الحسن أنه سمع: رسلنا لديهم [الزخرف/ 80] بإسكان اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vowel may be dropped as in ابن كثير's reading ويتقه; treating تقه like كتف/علم supports the same easing in ويصبر.
rows.anchor: ومما يقوي ذلك ويسوغ حمله عليه أنه قرأ: ويتقه [النور/ 52]

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read مرفق with kasra on mīm and fatḥa on fāʾ; al-Kisai also transmits the opposite vowel pattern through Abu Bakr from Asim.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي: مرفقا بكسر الميم

rows.speaker: نافع وابن عامر
rows.claim: They read مرفق with fatḥa on mīm and kasra on fāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن عامر: (مرفقا) بفتح الميم وكسر الفاء

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda says مرفق can mean something used for comfort or support; in the arm it names the elbow.
rows.anchor: أبو عبيدة: المرفق: ما ارتفقت به، وبعضهم يقول

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan treats both vowel patterns as lexical variants: مرفق can name an aid or be a noun like المسجد, without a difference in meaning.
rows.anchor: مرفقا ومرفقا: لغتان لا فرق بينهما أيضا، هما اسمان

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: They read تزاور with a doubled zāy; Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisai lighten it, while Ibn Amir reads تزور.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو: (تزاور) بتشديد الزاي

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda glosses تزاور عن كهفهم as inclining away from their cave, from the sense of ميل and انحراف.
rows.anchor: تميل عنه، وهو من الزور والأزور منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled form can result from deleting the second tāʾ, as deletion lightens a form much like assimilation; its sense is the sun's turning away to the right.
rows.anchor: من قال: تزاور حذف التاء الثانية، وخفف الكلمة بالحذف

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan says Ibn Amir's تزور does not normally mean the sun's inclination, but al-Farisi defends that sense with poetry using ازورار for turning away.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الحسن: لا يوضع في هذا المعنى

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع
rows.claim: They read ولملئت with a doubled lām and hamza; Ibn Kathir also has a reported light form through Ismail b. Muslim.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع: (ولملئت): مشددة مهموزة

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وعاصم وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read ولملئت with a light lām and hamza.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر وعاصم وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي: ولملئت خفيفة مهموزة

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan considers the light form more idiomatic; examples in poetry and امتلأت support this usage, though a heavy form is also attested in poetry.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الحسن: الخفيفة أجود في كلامهم، تقول: ملأتني رعبا

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم
rows.claim: They read بورقكم with kasra on rāʾ; Abu Amr, Hamza, and Abu Bakr from Asim use a quiescent rāʾ, and a report from Ruh describes assimilation.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم بورقكم مكسورة الراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both ورق and ورق are regular vowel variants; assimilating qāf into kāf is good because qāf is farther back and the following kāf nearer the mouth, favoring this direction of assimilation.
rows.anchor: ورق وورق: كنبد ونبد وكتف وكتف

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم
rows.claim: They read ثلاث مائة سنين with tanwin, while Hamza and al-Kisai make it a construct without tanwin.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم ثلاث مائة سنين منون

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan says the years belong to the three hundred; although العرب rarely add مائة to plural سنين, the construction is permissible, and Ibn Masud's codex has سنة singular.
rows.anchor: ولا يحسن إضافة المائة إلى السنين، لا تكاد العرب تقول: مائة سنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tanwin reading is sound because hundreds are usually annexed to singulars but can also be followed by plurals, as a cited poem demonstrates.
rows.anchor: أن هذا الضرب من العدد الذي يضاف في اللغة المشهورة إلى الآحاد
